extractedText: Sardines Turn Pricey as Gen Z Drives 30% Sales JumpInternational|Published 2026.08.30. 12:20:09|By Cho Su-yeonnewsuyeon@sedaily.com|Summary|SaveAAAAn AI-generated image created to help illustrate this articleSardines, long seen as a cheap and long-lasting staple, are commanding higher prices as young consumers embrace them as a health food. Demand is rising worldwide after the fish gained attention on social media, but shrinking catches in major producing countries have left some markets short of supply.Britain's Guardian recently reported that sardines are shifting from an inexpensive pantry item to a premium ingredient."Better Skin?" — Social Media Fuels the BoomTikTok and Instagram sit at the center of the sardine craze.Since last year, young consumers have taken up "sardinemaxxing," a trend of eating sardines in large quantities. Videos spread claiming that the fish, rich in protein and omega-3 fatty acids, helps overall health and skin care. Fashion trends followed, including "sardinecore" and "Sardine Girl Summer," built around clothing and bags printed with sardine motifs.Sales figures have shifted as well. Sardine sales in Britain rose about 30% over the past 12 months, according to Seafish, the country's public body for the seafood industry. Seafish said the "sardinemaxxing" trend circulating on social media may be one factor behind the increase.More extreme diets built solely around the fish have also emerged. Some social media users promote a so-called "sardine fast," eating almost nothing but sardines for several days. Nutrition experts have cautioned that relying on a single food can throw off nutritional balance.Clipart KoreaDemand Climbs as Moroccan Catches FallWhile more people are buying sardines, supply conditions have grown less stable.The Guardian reported that dwindling sardine stocks in Morocco, a leading producer, have combined with rising demand to create shortages at some supermarkets.Concern is also mounting inside Morocco. According to state broadcaster SNRT, sardine stocks have declined across multiple fishing grounds, cutting supply while domestic demand has stayed high and pushing prices up.The Moroccan government halted exports of frozen sardines in February to stabilize domestic supply. Morocco was the largest supplier of sardines imported into the European Union from outside the bloc in 2025, accounting for 91% of the value of those imports.Prices are also climbing in Portugal, often called the home of the sardine. In the Portuguese city of Matosinhos, dockside prices rose this year even though catches were relatively healthy. Local media reported that average auction prices for sardines have risen about 80% over the past two years.From Cheap Health Food to a Prized CatchThe appeal rests on nutrition and price at the same time. Sardines contain protein, omega-3 fatty acids and vitamins, yet cost less than salmon or tuna and keep for long periods in cans. That combination has made them an accessible health food for younger consumers facing higher living costs.Claims circulating on social media — that sardines improve skin, or that health benefits grow the more of them you eat — are a separate matter. Seafish stressed that the fish's nutritional merits should be distinguished from unverified health claims spreading online.As the craze continues, attention is turning to sustainable fishing. The Guardian noted that with climate change and declining fish stocks already weighing on supply, and social media adding to demand, consumers should look at where and how their sardines were caught rather than at the trend itself.#Sardines#Sardinemaxxing#GenZ#Omega3#Seafood#Morocco#FoodTrendsOriginal reporting by Cho Su-yeon for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
